title: The Month the Markets Recalibrated
standfirst: A war in the Gulf jolted energy markets, central banks split in opposite directions, and the world's first trillionaire was minted — as the World Bank cut global growth to its slowest since the pandemic.
editorsNote: June 2026 revived a word economists had hoped to retire: stagflation. Growth is fading even as prices keep climbing — the hardest problem in macroeconomics, because the usual medicine for one ailment worsens the other.

indicators.label: Global growth, 2026
indicators.note: World Bank — weakest since the pandemic

highlights.title: The slowest world since the pandemic
highlights.blurb: The World Bank cut 2026 global growth to 2.5%, blaming an energy shock and the US–Iran conflict. S&P went lower at 2.2%; the OECD landed at 2.8%. They disagree on the decimal, not the direction.

highlights.title: The hawks take flight
highlights.blurb: The ECB raised rates 25bp on 11 June — the first G7 tightening of 2026 — and the Bank of Japan matched it. India held at 5.25%; Brazil kept easing. One month, two opposite diagnoses.

highlights.title: The strait that moved the world economy
highlights.blurb: A conflict involving the US and Iran put the Strait of Hormuz back at the centre of every forecast. Analysts warned $150-a-barrel oil could tip the world into recession.

highlights.title: The AI trade wobbles
highlights.blurb: A global tech sell-off led by AI and chip stocks rippled from Wall Street into Asia, deepened by a hawkish read of the Fed's June meeting.

highlights.title: The first trillionaire
highlights.blurb: SpaceX's IPO carried Elon Musk's net worth to roughly $1.2 trillion — a fortune equal to about 3% of the entire US economy.

highlights.title: When AI shows up in your electricity bill
highlights.blurb: Data-centre build-out, a chip shortage and rising software subscriptions are lifting prices — an inflation born of a scramble for compute, not consumer excess.
